title: Shemini Atzeret: stay one more day
hookLine: Rashi: like a king who asks his children to stay one more day

lines: THE BAGS ARE BY THE DOOR.
cards: The bags are by the door. The car is packed. Somebody has already said, we should really get going.
And then a grandmother, or an aunt, or a parent who doesn't say this kind of thing out loud, says: stay. Just one more night. Nothing planned, no outing, no big meal.
They just aren't ready for the house to be empty yet. The Torah's festival calendar has a day like that, right at the end of Sukkot.
It has few rituals of its own, and a well-known explanation of it is a story about a family that doesn't want to say goodbye.

teach.b: Shemini Atzeret means the eighth day of assembly.
In the old Jewish translation of Leviticus, after seven days of Sukkot, "on the eighth day shall be a holy convocation unto you," and then: "it is a day of solemn assembly." That's the word atzeret.
Rashi hears in it holding back: I have held you here with me. Here's the strange part.

teach.h: NO BOOTH, NO LULAV, NO WILLOWS.
teach.b: The eighth day has no sukkah requirement, no lulav, no willows. In the Land of Israel, people step out of the booth and back into the house. So what is the day for?
Rashi answers with a parable drawn from the midrash. A king invites his children to a feast for a set number of days. When it's time for them to leave, he says: your parting is hard for me.

teach.h: A KING SAYS: STAY ONE MORE DAY.
teach.b: Please, stay one more day. That's the whole holiday. A week of crowds, guests, palm branches and booths, then one quiet day that's only about being together.

Over the seven days of Sukkot, the Temple offered seventy bulls, and the rabbis connected those seventy to the seventy nations of the world. On the eighth day, a single bull: a small, private meal after the big banquet.
Today the day has one notable addition. In the standing prayer, people begin to mention rain, and many synagogues chant a special prayer for it. Winter is coming in the Land of Israel.
The asking begins on the day when nobody is in a hurry to leave.

how: Shemini Atzeret is a full festival day after Sukkot, kept with festive meals and synagogue services; the prayer for rain (Tefillat Geshem) is chanted, and the mention of rain enters the daily Amidah from that day until Passover.

games.q: you're the king in Rashi's parable. the feast is over and your children are at the door. what do you say?
o: thank you for coming, safe travels.
your parting is hard for me. stay one more day.
come back next year with more guests.
games.why: the king asks them to stay one more day. that, Rashi says, is Shemini Atzeret: a day that exists only for being together.

practice: Bring one person you love to mind, near or far, and picture the last time you said goodbye, how quickly it went. Now imagine you stayed: no plan, no agenda, just the two of you in the same room. Breathe with that.

wordCard.voice: Shemini Atzeret. The eighth day of assembly, the day God, in Rashi's parable, asks the children to stay. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the eighth day of assembly. atzeret comes from a root of holding back and staying.
